name: Olbers' Paradox
statement: If the universe were infinite and eternal, the night sky would blaze as bright as the Sun.
meaning: Olbers' paradox asks why the night sky is dark. In an infinite, eternal, static universe uniformly filled with stars, every line of sight would eventually meet the surface of a star, so the whole sky should shine as brightly as the Sun. A star's brightness falls with the square of distance, but the number of stars at a given distance grows with the square of distance, so the two effects cancel and every shell of sky contributes equally. The observed darkness contradicts this, and that contradiction is the paradox.
mechanism: Sum the light from concentric shells of stars around us: each shell is dimmer per star but holds proportionally more stars, so each contributes the same amount, and infinitely many shells would give an infinitely bright, or at least stellar-surface-bright, sky. The resolution is that the universe is neither eternal nor static. It has a finite age, so light from very distant stars has not had time to reach us and the observable universe holds only finitely many stars, far too few to fill the sky. Cosmic expansion also redshifts distant light, weakening it further, but that is the secondary effect.

examples.text: Doubling the distance to a shell of stars quarters each star's brightness but quadruples the number of stars, so every shell adds the same light — the heart of the paradox.
Because the universe is about 13.8 billion years old and light travels at finite speed, we see only a finite sphere of stars, whose combined light leaves the sky dark.
Edgar Allan Poe, in his 1848 prose poem Eureka, sketched the modern idea that the sky is dark because light from the most distant regions has not yet reached us.

variants.name: The redshift contribution
variants.text: Cosmic expansion stretches distant starlight toward longer wavelengths and dims it, shifting relic light into the microwave band; a real but secondary factor, too small alone to explain the darkness.

variants.name: Evidence for a beginning
variants.text: The paradox's resolution is often read as simple evidence, needing no telescope, that the universe had a beginning rather than being infinitely old and static.

whyItMatters: It is a rare case where the plainest observation, that night is dark, constrains the structure of the cosmos. Requiring only that you look up, it argues against an infinite, eternal, static universe and sits comfortably with a universe of finite age, making it a memorable pointer toward Big Bang cosmology and a classic demonstration that simple questions can carry deep answers.

working.text: treat the dark night sky as a genuine constraint on cosmology, not a triviality, since an infinite static universe predicts otherwise.
explain the darkness first by the universe's finite age and finite observable extent, the primary resolution.
include cosmic expansion and redshift as a real but secondary dimming, not the main answer.

limits: The observation is a plain fact; the resolution rests on well-established Big Bang cosmology, with the finite age of the universe as the decisive factor and expansion-driven redshift as a smaller contributor. Quantitative analyses find redshift alone dims the background by only a factor of a few, far too little to account for the darkness. The paradox specifically assumes an infinite population of stars, and it is the finite observable portion, set by finite age, that resolves it.
misreadings: Intervening dust does not resolve it: over eternity the dust would heat up and re-radiate the absorbed starlight, eventually glowing as brightly as the stars, so absorption only delays the problem. Redshift and expansion alone do not resolve it either; they contribute only modestly, and the primary answer is the universe's finite age. And the darkness is not explained by there simply being few stars, but by our seeing only a finite sphere of an assumed-infinite universe.
origin: Named after the German astronomer Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers, who discussed it in 1823, though the puzzle was raised earlier by Kepler, Halley, and de Chéseaux; the finite-age resolution was developed through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
